newsitem.title: USA: Steady savers win the fund wars.
newsitem.headline: Steady savers win the fund wars.

text.p: Most fund investors spend considerable time trying to identify funds that will win the performance derby. But many of them forget that the growth of their savings in the long term depends on other factors as well.

The most important factor is how much money they invest in their fund portfolios. A person who invests $10,000 in mutual funds that return 8 pecent annually will have $100,626 after 30 years. That compares with only $50,313 for someone who put $5,000 to work at the same time and earned the same returns.

The second factor is when you invest the money. Many analysts spend their careers trying to figure out when investors should be in technology stocks, junk bonds, overseas investments or money market funds. But study after study has shown that even the pros have a great deal of trouble making the right timing calls.
Worse, market timers generally run up large trading costs in the course of trying to accomplish that goal.
Fortunately, the best timing methods are the simplest. All you have to do is follow two rules:

Rule No. 1: Start early. Let's say you begin investing at age 25, putting $2,000 into mutual funds in an IRA each year. After 10 years, you stop making contributions to your IRA. Assuming your investment earns 8 pecent annually, your $20,000 investment will grow to $314,870 by age 65.

Now, assume your friend waits until age 35 to start saving -- but makes $2,000 contributions annually to an IRA for 30 years. At an 8 pecent annual return, the $60,000 investment will grow to only $244,691 by age 65. In other words, you come out with more money even though you saved only one-third as much as your friend. And that's all because you got an early start.

Rule No. 2: Make regular contributions to your fund. Most financial planners recommend making a regular monthly contribution to your savings in mutual funds -- whether those savings are in a retirement plan at work or in a separate account. There are at least six reasons why that advice makes sense.

First, it makes investing easy. More than 6,200 funds offer automatic investment programmes that will sweep a fixed sum from your bank account to one or more mutual funds each month, according to Morningstar. You don't have to remember to write the check each month -- in fact, you don't even have to think about doing it.

Second, a programme of contributing regularly to your funds takes the guesswork out of investing. You don't have to worry anymore about whether you should buy or sell stocks, bonds or other investments right now -- a choice that you and your broker will probably get wrong, anyway.

Third, such a programme means you will continue to invest when prices are declining. And that, of course, is the best time to invest. For example, say the stock market declines 20 pecent next month. Many investors will rush to sell their shares in mutual funds -- especially those that suffer the greatest losses. Meanwhile, you will continue to buy shares at a steady pace.

What if stocks keep declining? You'll keep buying at ever-lower prices, reducing your average cost per share. That will pay off in the long run when stocks recover, provided you keep making your steady investments. By contrast, investors who abandon stocks during such a downturn will wait until prices recover to buy back into the market. They'll likely miss the biggest gains, which often come suddenly and frequently occur in the earliest stages of a new bull market.

Fourth reason: You don't have to come up with all of the money at once. Some analysts argue that you can make more money if you simply put a lump sum in a fund today and then let it grow over time, rather than delaying your investment. But most of us must do our saving a little bit at a time, and regular investing works well under those conditions.

Regular investing also reduces risk. An investor who puts a large sum to work all at once risks seeing his money dwindle dramatically in a market downturn. By contrast, if you spread your investment out over time, you will spread your risk out as well.

Finally, regular investing can reduce the entry price for many funds. Typically, you'll need $1,000 to $3,000 or more to meet minimum investment requirements imposed by fund sponsors. But more than 40 families offer at least one fund with no sales charge that requires a minimum monthly investment of $50 or less. Among them: Artisan Partners (800-344-1770); Janus Capital (800-525-8983); and T. Rowe Price Associates (800-638-5660).
(EDITORS: Clint Willis is a freelance writer who covers financial issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Willis.)
